item.title: “Monks, just as an oil lamp burns in dependence on oil and a wick, and someone occasionally pours in oil and adjusts the wick —…
item.description:
“Monks, just as an oil lamp burns in dependence on oil and a wick, and someone occasionally pours in oil and adjusts the wick — that oil lamp, being nourished and sustained in such a way, would burn for a long time. So too, monks, one who dwells seeing gratification in things that are fetters — craving increases. With craving as condition, clinging arises … Thus the origination of this whole mass of suffering. Monks, just as an oil lamp burns in dependence on oil and a wick, and no one occasionally pours in oil or adjusts the wick — that oil lamp, being without its own fuel, with no further fuel added, not being nourished, would be extinguished. So too, monks, one who dwells seeing peril in things that are fetters — craving ceases. With the cessation of craving, clinging ceases … Thus the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.54
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, there are these five strands of sensual pleasure. What five? Forms cognizable by the eye — desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing;…
item.description:
“Monks, there are these five strands of sensual pleasure. What five? Forms cognizable by the eye — desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing; sounds cognizable by the ear … odors … tastes … touches cognizable by the body — desirable … enticing. These, monks, are the five strands of sensual pleasure. To abandon these five strands of sensual pleasure, monks, the four foundations of mindfulness should be developed.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 9.65
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, here a monk, when there is sensual desire in him, knows: ‘There is sensual desire in me’; or when there is no sensual desire…
item.description:
“Monks, here a monk, when there is sensual desire in him, knows: ‘There is sensual desire in me’; or when there is no sensual desire in him, knows: ‘There is no sensual desire in me.’ And he knows how unarisen sensual desire arises; he knows how arisen sensual desire is abandoned; and he knows how abandoned sensual desire does not arise in the future.”

From: Dīgha Nikāya 22 – Mahāsatipaṭṭhānasutta
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “And what, monks, is the noble search? Here, monks, a person being himself subject to birth, having known the peril in what is subject to…
item.description:
“And what, monks, is the noble search? Here, monks, a person being himself subject to birth, having known the peril in what is subject to birth, seeks the unborn, supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna; being himself subject to aging, having known the peril in aging, seeks the unaging, supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna; being subject to sickness … the unailing … subject to death … the deathless … subject to sorrow … the sorrowless … subject to defilement, having known the peril in defilement, seeks the undefiled, supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna. This, monks, is called the noble search.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 26 – Ariyapariyesanāsutta
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, if wanderers of other sects ask you: ‘For what purpose, friends, is the holy life lived under the ascetic Gotama?’ — being asked thus,…
item.description:
“Monks, if wanderers of other sects ask you: ‘For what purpose, friends, is the holy life lived under the ascetic Gotama?’ — being asked thus, monks, you should answer them: ‘For the purpose of the destruction of greed, friends, the holy life is lived under the Blessed One.’ Then, monks, if they ask: ‘Is there, friends, a path, a way for the destruction of greed?’ — being asked thus, you should answer: ‘There is a path, a way for the destruction of greed.’ And what, monks, is that path, that way? It is the Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view … right concentration. This, monks, is the path, the way for the destruction of greed. Being asked thus, monks, you should answer them in that way.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 45.41
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Then I, after some time, having known as they actually are the origination, the passing away, the gratification, the peril, and the escape in the…
item.description:
“Then I, after some time, having known as they actually are the origination, the passing away, the gratification, the peril, and the escape in the case of sensual pleasures, abandoned craving for sensual pleasures, removed the fever for sensual pleasures, and dwelt with craving cut off, with mind inwardly peaceful. Then I saw other beings who had not abandoned lust for sensual pleasures being consumed by craving for sensual pleasures, being burned by the fever of sensual pleasures, indulging in sensual pleasures. I did not envy them, nor did I delight in that. Why is that? Because, Māgandiya, there is this pleasure and rapture, apart from sensual pleasures, apart from unwholesome states, and having attained the heavenly pleasure, I dwell delighting in that. I do not envy what is inferior, nor do I delight in that.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 75 – Māgandiyasutta
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, I have searched for the gratification of form. Whatever gratification there is in form — I have found it. To what extent there is…
item.description:
“Monks, I have searched for the gratification of form. Whatever gratification there is in form — I have found it. To what extent there is gratification in form — that I have seen well with wisdom. Monks, I have searched for the peril of form. Whatever peril there is in form — I have found it. To what extent there is peril in form — that I have seen well with wisdom. Monks, I have searched for the escape from form. Whatever escape there is from form — I have found it. To what extent there is escape from form — that I have seen well with wisdom. Monks, I have searched for the gratification of feeling … of perception … of formations … of consciousness. Whatever gratification there is in consciousness — I have found it. To what extent there is gratification in consciousness — that I have seen well with wisdom. Monks, I have searched for the peril of consciousness … the escape from consciousness … That I have seen well with wisdom. Monks, as long as I did not directly know as it actually is the gratification as gratification, the peril as peril, the escape as escape in regard to these five aggregates of clinging, I did not declare that … ascetics, brahmins, devas, and humans. But when I directly knew them, then the knowledge and vision arose in me: ‘My mind is liberated, imperturbable. This is my last life, now there is no further becoming.’”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.27
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, an untaught ordinary person might become disenchanted, dispassionate, and liberated regarding this body composed of the four great elements. Why is that? Because he…
item.description:
“Monks, an untaught ordinary person might become disenchanted, dispassionate, and liberated regarding this body composed of the four great elements. Why is that? Because he sees this body composed of the four great elements increasing and decreasing, being taken up and discarded. Therefore, an untaught ordinary person might become disenchanted, dispassionate, and liberated regarding it. But regarding that which is called mind, intellect, consciousness — here, an untaught ordinary person is not capable of disenchantment, not capable of dispassion, not capable of liberation. Why is that? For a long time, monks, an untaught ordinary person has been attached, regarded as ‘mine,’ grasped at: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self.’ Therefore, he is not capable of disenchantment, dispassion, or liberation regarding it.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.61
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, what is Right Mindfulness? Monks, here a monk abides contemplating the body as a body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having restrained covetousness and sorrow…
item.description:
“Monks, what is Right Mindfulness? Monks, here a monk abides contemplating the body as a body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having restrained covetousness and sorrow in the world; abides contemplating feelings as feelings … mind as mind … phenomena as phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having restrained covetousness and sorrow in the world. This, monks, is called Right Mindfulness.”

From: Dīgha Nikāya 22 – Mahāsatipaṭṭhānasutta

item.title: Sitting down to one side, that monk said to the Venerable Sāriputta: “Venerable Sāriputta, a monk who is my companion has abandoned the training and…
item.description:
Sitting down to one side, that monk said to the Venerable Sāriputta: “Venerable Sāriputta, a monk who is my companion has abandoned the training and returned to the lower life.” - “That comes to be, friend, for one who does not guard the sense faculties, does not know moderation in eating, and is not committed to wakefulness. For such a person, it is impossible that he would continue the perfectly pure holy life for his whole life. Friend, a monk who does guard the sense faculties, knows moderation in eating, and is committed to wakefulness — it is possible that he would continue the perfectly pure holy life for his whole life. Therefore, friend, you should train thus: ‘We will guard the sense faculties, know moderation in eating, and be committed to wakefulness.’ Thus, friend, you should train.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.120
